page: Google Cloud Platform n4-standard-48 is a general-purpose server instance featuring 48 vCPUs mapped to 24 physical Intel cores with hyper-threading enabled. Built on the x86_64 architecture, the processor includes a 260 MB L3 cache, 2 MB L2 cache, and 48 KB L1d cache. The system is equipped with 192 GB of system memory, providing a balanced allocation of 4.0 GB of RAM per vCPU. This instance does not include local storage or dedicated GPU hardware.

The underlying Intel processor supports advanced instruction sets, including Advanced Vector Extensions (AVX-512) and Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) for tile and int8 operations. Cryptographic acceleration is supported via AES, VAES, and SHA_NI flags. In benchmark evaluations, the instance demonstrates strong performance in multi-core workloads, achieving top-quartile results in Geekbench multi-core testing, software compilation with Clang, ray tracing, and image processing. Passmark CPU tests also place its extended instructions, encryption, and physics capabilities in the top 25% tier.

Memory performance is characterized by strong uncached large-block read and write bandwidth, measuring 259.28 GB/sec and 114.19 GB/sec respectively, while small-block cached reads perform within the average range. The instance delivers strong throughput for static web serving and database operations. For machine learning workloads, the hardware-assisted matrix extensions contribute to strong prompt processing speeds for small and medium LLM models, though text generation speeds for larger models remain in the average tier.

From a resource density perspective, the n4-standard-48 offers a balanced hardware profile that avoids the premium costs associated with specialized memory-optimized or GPU-accelerated instances. The lack of bundled local storage requires external block storage attachment, which represents a key architectural tradeoff. This server is highly suited for multi-threaded general-purpose workloads, including software compilation pipelines, database operations, static web serving, and CPU-based machine learning inference.
